source_text: Aperit se Apostolus clarius in processu et docet in perditione salutis humanae Deum copia suae miserationis admonitum desperatis rebus efficaciorem solito medicinam tulisse, ut quos praeceptis non correxerat, beneficiis obligaret et ita devotionem exigeret in futurum, ut non imputaret peracta, studerentque deinceps custodire iustitiam homines, quam compendio credulitatis fuerant assecuti. Abundantia ergo praecedentium peccatorum tam abundantis misericordiae exegit auxilium, quoniam, nisi tanta copia indulgentis fuisset, nulla alia disciplina morbis tam gravibus subveniret. Verum in hac divini commendatione beneficii vidit Apostolus obiectioni locum patere eorum, qui dicere poterant: Si rite merita causarum de effectibus aestimamus, et peccatorum copia, ut misericordia Dei afflueret, impetravit; insistendum peccatis est, ut gratiae non desit ubertas. Occurrens itaque opinioni eiusmodi: Quid ergo dicemus? - inquit - permanebimus in peccato, ut gratia abundet? Absit! Qui enim mortui sumus peccato, quemadmodum adhuc vivemus in eo? An ignoratis, quoniam quicumque baptizati sumus in Christo Iesu, in mortem illius baptizati sumus? Consepulti ergo sumus illi per baptismum in mortem, ut quemadmodum surrexit Christus in gloria Patris, ita et nos in novitate vitae ambulemus [n372] .
pass_a_gloss: The Apostle opens himself more clearly in the progress and teaches that in the perdition of human salvation God, warned by a plenty of his pity, brought a medicine more effective than usual to desperate things, so that those whom he had not corrected by precepts he would bind by benefits and so would exact devotion in the future that he would not impute things done, and human beings would thereafter strive to guard the justice which they had obtained by a shortcut of belief. The abundance therefore of preceding sins exacted the help of so abundant a mercy, since, unless there had been so great a plenty of one indulging, no other discipline would come to help diseases so grave. But in this commendation of the divine benefit the Apostle saw a place lie open for the objection of those who could say: If we rightly estimate the deserts of causes from effects, even a plenty of sins obtained that the mercy of God would flow; one must insist on sins, so that richness may not fail grace. Occurring therefore to an opinion of this kind: What therefore shall we say? he says — shall we remain in sin, so that grace may abound? Far be it! For we who have died to sin, how shall we still live in it? Or do you not know that whoever we have been baptized in Christ Jesus, we have been baptized into his death? Buried together therefore with him through baptism into death, so that as Christ rose in the glory of the Father, so also we may walk in newness of life.

LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'
LS meritum=desert; Blaise without later merit-system
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: As he proceeds, the apostle explains himself more clearly. He teaches that, when human salvation was being lost, God, moved by the abundance of his compassion, brought a medicine more effective than usual to a desperate situation. Those whom he had not corrected by commands he would bind to himself by benefits, requiring devotion for the future while not imputing past deeds. People should then strive to preserve the righteousness they had obtained by the direct path of belief. The abundance of preceding sins therefore called for the help of such abundant mercy: unless the forgiver’s generosity had been so great, no other discipline could have helped diseases so serious. But in commending this divine benefit, the apostle saw room for an objection from people who might say: ‘If we rightly assess the worth of causes by their effects, and the abundance of sins obtained an outpouring of God’s mercy, we should persist in sins so that grace’s abundance does not fail.’ Anticipating such an opinion, he says: ‘What, then, shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? Far from it! For we who died to sin, how shall we still live in it? Or do you not know that all of us baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose in the Father’s glory, we too might walk in newness of life’ (Romans 6:1–4).

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)
